title: Closures, escaping and capture lists
summary: A closure is a function you can store and pass around. It remembers the variables it uses. `@escaping` means it may run later, after the function returns.
body: **In simple words:** A closure is a small piece of code you hand to someone to run later, like a callback. It "captures" (remembers) the variables it uses from around it.
**Real-life analogy:** Leaving a note for a colleague: "when the parcel arrives, call me". The note (closure) remembers your phone number (captured variable) and is used later.

**Escaping vs non-escaping:** By default a closure parameter is non-escaping: it must run before the function returns (e.g. `map`, `filter`). Non-escaping closures cannot cause retain cycles and are cheaper. `@escaping` means the function stores it or calls it later (network callbacks, completion handlers). Escaping closures are where `[weak self]` matters.
**Capture by reference vs value:** Without a capture list, the closure sees the latest value of the variable. With `[x]` it takes a snapshot of `x` at creation time.
**Swift 6:** closures that cross threads/actors must be `@Sendable`, which means they cannot capture mutable local variables. This prevents data races.
keyPoints: Closures capture variables by reference by default; a capture list `[x]` copies the value at creation.
Non-escaping is the default for parameters; `@escaping` closures may be stored and run later.
Retain cycles only happen with escaping closures stored by the object they capture.
`@Sendable` closures cannot capture mutable state, which keeps concurrent code safe.

followups: **Why are escaping closures more expensive?** Their captured context must live on the heap.
**What is a trailing closure?** Writing the last closure argument outside the parentheses: `items.map { $0.name }`.
**What is an autoclosure?** A parameter that wraps an expression in a closure so it is evaluated lazily, e.g. `assert(condition())` and `??`.
